Added to your notes.

### Summary of error handling chat · 2 Nov

Two kinds of failure: a bug panics, an expected problem returns Result. Panic unwinds the stack and runs Drop, then the thread ends.

Result is an enum Ok(T) / Err(E). Callers must handle both cases. Shortcuts like unwrap, expect, unwrap_or, ok_or, map_err change how you handle the error.

The ? operator: on Ok(v) / Some(v) the expression becomes v and the function carries on; on Err(e) / None it returns early from the nearest function with Err(From::from(e)). The conversion is From::from(e) into the error type the enclosing function promises.

In question_mark.rs first_number returns Result<i64, Box<dyn Error>>. Line 14 `ok_or("empty line")?` converts a &str error into Box<dyn Error> via From. Line 15 `first.parse()?` converts a ParseIntError into Box<dyn Error> via From. The target type is fixed by the function signature, not by the error itself.

Box<dyn Error> hides the concrete type. downcast_ref::<ParseIntError>() on a Box<dyn Error> only succeeds when the boxed concrete error is actually a ParseIntError. For first_number("twelve apples") the error comes from parse, so downcast_ref returns Some and prints true. For first_number("") the error comes from ok_or("empty line")? so the box holds a different error and downcast_ref::<ParseIntError>() returns None.

main can return Result<(), E>. Then ? works in main and an Err is printed to stderr with exit code 1, not 101.

answer_text:
Deref coercion only changes the type of a reference, it does not change how many references exist.

`&T` is a shared reference. If `T: Deref<Target = U>` the compiler can insert `&T -> &U` by calling `Deref::deref` and borrowing the target. That is still a shared borrow, so aliasing is preserved.

`&mut U` is an exclusive borrow. If `&T` could become `&mut U` you would get exclusive access through a shared reference. That would break the rule that a mutable reference must be unique.

Look at `deref.rs` lines 35-41. `name` is `MyBox<String>` and it is `mut`. `name.push_str("acean")` works because the compiler does `&mut MyBox<String> -> &mut String` via `DerefMut`. The `mut` on `name` is what gives you the exclusive borrow.

TRY this to see the rule in action: in `deref.rs` change line 35 to `let name = MyBox(String::from("Rust"));` removing `mut`, then try to compile. `push_str` needs `&mut String`, and the compiler will refuse to turn an immutable `&MyBox<String>` into `&mut String`.

That is why the table in lesson §5 says `&T -> &mut U` is never allowed.

answer_text:
The boundary is the crate boundary, not just the file.

In `src/lib.rs` the unit tests are a child module of the same crate:

```rust
// src/lib.rs lines 64-66
fn sum(values: &[f64]) -> f64 { ... }   // private

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {                              // line 69
    use super::*;                        // line 70
```

`mod tests` is inside `lib.rs`, so it is a child of the parent module. In Rust a child module can use its parent's private items. `use super::*;` brings those items into the test module's scope, which is why `private_sum_works` can call `sum` even though `sum` is not `pub`.

Integration tests are different. Look at `tests/public_api.rs`:

```rust
// tests/public_api.rs lines 130-133
// Each file in tests/ is a separate crate that sees only the public API.
mod common;

#[test]
fn fractions_of_shared_scores() { ... stats::to_fraction ... }
```

Each file in `tests/` is compiled as its own crate that depends on `stats`. The library it links to is built the normal way, without `cfg(test)`, and it only exports `pub` items. So `stats::sum` is invisible, and the compiler gives `error[E0603]: function sum is private`.

That is why the same `use super::*;` trick works for unit tests but cannot make private items visible to integration tests.

Yes. That is exactly the difference.

Unit tests are inside the crate, compiled with `cfg(test)` on, so they see everything that is `#[cfg(test)]` in `src/`. That is why `mod tests` at line 68 of `src/lib.rs` can `use super::*;` at line 70 and call the private `sum` at line 64.

Integration tests in `tests/` are separate crates. Cargo builds the `stats` library for them the normal way, without `cfg(test)`. So a `pub` item marked `#[cfg(test)]` is compiled out of that build and does not exist for the integration test crate at all.
